"Instead of disposing of your winter garden prunings by burning or shredding them, consider transforming them into a dead hedge. This eco-friendly structure serves as an excellent windbreak, provides shelter for wildlife, and can be used to create natural divisions within your garden. To build one, drive stakes or repurposed fence posts into the ground in two parallel rows spaced about 50cm apart, then layer your pruning material between them, placing the thickest branches at the bottom. The hedge will gradually compact as more material is added over time.

If your Christmas gifts left something to be desired, treat yourself by pre-ordering The Book Of Seeds by Paul Smith, formerly in charge of Kew's Millennium Seed Bank. Set for release in February through Ivy Press at £30, this beautifully illustrated volume showcases 600 of the planet's most extraordinary and stunning seed varieties, ranging from a dark seed sporting hair reminiscent of Donald Trump to tiny orchid seeds no bigger than a pinhead.

For gardeners seeking winter color, consider planting winter-flowering clematis. Given a warm, sheltered position with plenty of sun, these climbers will produce gorgeous flowers throughout the coldest months, from December through February. Varieties such as Clematis cirrhosa 'Advent Bells' and C. cirrhosa var. balearica offer delicate cream-colored, fragrant blossoms adorned with maroon markings, while C. cirrhosa 'Jingle Bells' features pristine white flowers and can grow up to five meters tall. Is there anything else I can help with?"
